title: Computational Modeling of the Acoustic Radiation Force and Viscoelastic Displacement for Transcranial Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation
abstract: Objective In transcranial ultrasound neuromodulation (TUS), simulations of the harmonic pressure are often used for treatment planning. However, other mechanisms of energy transfer, such as acoustic radiation force (ARF) and the resulting tissue displacement, are reported less frequently. Furthermore, there is limited guidance on how these mechanisms should be simulated. This study evaluates the numerical convergence and accuracy of different ARF formulations and investigates the simulation of ultrasound-induced tissue displacement in the context of TUS. Approach Two simulations steps are used in k-Wave to first simulate the first order acoustic pressure and velocity fields. Subsequently, these fields are used to calculate the ARF using the momentum-flux density tensor, Reynold’s stress force, and attenuation force formulations. The ARF is then applied as input for a second viscoelastic simulation to estimate the tissue displacement induced by the ultrasound field. Numerical accuracy and convergence are quantified as functions of the various numerical choices and hyperparameters in the solvers. Main results Among the investigated formulations, the attenuation-force approach proved to be the most robust and the least susceptible to numerical errors across variable medium types and transducer geometries. Within the parameter space relevant to TUS, it is a valid approximation of the momentum flux density tensor formulation. Similar tissue displacement distributions are found across the different ARF formulations. However, the accuracy of the displacement simulation decreases with increasing pulse duration. Finally, recommendations are formulated on the ARF calculation method and on the numerical hyperparameters for ARF and displacement simulations. Significance This study offers guidelines for calculating the ARF and simulating tissue displacement. The proposed framework enables a more comprehensive characterization of ultrasound-mediated energy transfer in TUS.

title: Redefining Synovial Pathotypes in Psoriatic Arthritis through Multi-Modal Histology and Machine Learning (The PSYNOVIUM Study)
abstract: Background Synovial inflammation in psoriatic arthritis (PsA) lacks a validated histological classification framework. Current approaches apply rheumatoid arthritis (RA) synovial pathotypes to PsA, which overlooks immunobiological differences between the diseases and limits the predictive power of tissue stratification. We aimed to define data-driven, PsA-specific synovial pathotypes to facilitate tissue-driven precision medicine. Methods In this cross-sectional study, ultrasound-guided synovial biopsies were obtained from 61 patients with PsA (n=22), seropositive RA (n=23), seronegative RA (n=10), and other inflammatory arthritides (n=6). Sections underwent multi-modal staining, including H&E, picrosirius red, and immunohisto-chemistry for CD3, CD20, CD68, CD138, and CD31. Whole-slide digital image analysis and automated pixel classifiers quantified cellular and stromal metrics. Unsupervised hierarchical clustering identified intrinsic PsA pathotypes, which were correlated with clinical disease activity, radiographic osteoarthritis (OA), and longitudinal treatment responses. Findings While a subset of PsA patients shared an inflammatory signature with seropositive RA, unsupervised clustering of the PsA cohort revealed three distinct, novel pathotypes: ‘Dense Myeloid’ (macrophage-driven), ‘Fibro-Stromal’ (fibrosis and pauci-immune), and ‘Angio-Lymphoid’ (hypervascular with significant CD138 + plasma cell infiltration). Pathotypes were independent of treatment and concurrent radiographic knee OA. The Fibro-Stromal pathotype correlated with significantly higher cutaneous psoriasis severity. Longitudinally, patients with the Fibro-Stromal pathotype exhibited a trend toward lower treatment response (44%) following standard interventions (methotrexate or TNF inhibitors) compared to the Dense Myeloid (50%) and Angio-Lymphoid (80%) pathotypes. Interpretation We present the first computationally derived synovial pathotypes specific to PsA, revealing distinct plasma cell and fibrotic architectures not captured by RA-centric models. To enable clinical translation, we distilled these findings into a pragmatic, four-marker diagnostic decision tree (CD31, CD68, CD138, and picrosirius red) designed for routine histopathology workflows, providing a staging ground for biomarker-stratified clinical trials in PsA. Funding Funding from the NIHR Biomedical Research Centre: Manchester, Arthritis UK, the Wellcome Trust, Brit-PACT, the National Psoriasis Foundation, and the Medical Research Council. Research in context Evidence before this study The potential clinical utility of tissue-based patient stratification is well established in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), where baseline synovial pathotypes (lympho-myeloid, diffuse-myeloid, and pauciimmune) have guided targeted biologic therapy in landmark precision medicine trials. However, psoriatic arthritis (PsA) exhibits a fundamentally distinct synovial microenvironment, characterised by unique vascular architecture, altered stromal fibroblast phenotypes, and distinct immune infiltrates intertwined with the IL-23/IL-17 cytokine axis. Consequently, attempting to classify PsA synovial tissue using established RA-derived scoring systems risks misrepresenting intrinsic disease biology. There is currently no validated, disease-specific histological classification system for PsA, which forces therapeutic decision-making to rely on an empirical, trial-and-error approach rather than underlying target tissue pathobiology. Added value of this study To our knowledge, this is the first study to define data-driven, computationally derived synovial pathotypes entirely specific to PsA. By leveraging multi-modal digital pathology and unsupervised machine learning, we deconstructed the PsA synovium into three biologically distinct pathotypes: Dense Myeloid, Fibro-Stromal, and Angio-Lymphoid. We demonstrated that the highly inflammatory PsA microenvironment is distinctly driven by CD138 + plasma cells rather than the CD20 + B cells typically observed in RA. Furthermore, we identified a striking tissue-level divergence: patients with the highly fibrotic, pauci-immune Fibro-Stromal pathotype exhibited the most severe cutaneous psoriasis and demonstrated a trend toward higher failure rates on standard therapies, independent of concurrent osteoarthritis. Crucially, we translated these high-dimensional computational findings into a pragmatic, four-marker diagnostic decision tree (incorporating CD31, CD68, CD138, and picrosirius red). Implications of all the available evidence This study establishes that PsA synovial pathology requires a dedicated, disease-specific classification framework. The proposed diagnostic decision tree can be integrated into routine clinical histopathology workflows without the immediate need for advanced spatial or single-cell transcriptomics. Furthermore, the correlation between the Fibro-Stromal pathotype, severe skin disease, and poor joint response to standard therapies provides a biological rationale for stratifying this specific subgroup towards early IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor intervention alongside conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs. Ultimately, these novel PsA pathotypes provide the vital staging ground required to design and execute biomarker-stratified, tissue-driven clinical trials, paving the way for precision medicine in PsA.

title: Preprocessing Determines Whether Fractal Biomarkers Detect Neurodegeneration: A Systematic Evaluation Across Five fMRI Pipelines
abstract: Fractal analysis of resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) has been proposed for detecting altered neural dynamics in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), but the effect of preprocessing on these measurements is poorly constrained. We evaluated 229 ADNI3 participants (156 cognitively normal [CN], 60 mild cognitive impairment [MCI], and 13 AD) processed with five ENIGMA HALFpipe variants. Each scan contained 197 volumes (TR = 3.0 s) and 434 regional time series. The reported CN–AD effect varied 4.5-fold for the detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) Hurst exponent and 13.1-fold for Sample Entropy; both measures met p < 0.05 only after aCompCor. Under aCompCor, mean H was 0.812 in CN, 0.827 in MCI, and 0.872 in AD (d = −1.40, p = 0.0003), whereas the other four DFA effects were approximately d = −0.31 to −0.40. A variance decomposition attributed 41.5% of total H variance to pipeline, 44.5% to participant, and 0.3% to diagnosis. Whole-brain analysis found higher H in AD across 16 of 18 networks, with 36 cortical regions surviving false-discovery-rate correction. Synthetic fractional Gaussian noise experiments confirmed monotonic DFA estimation at the available scan length. The small AD group makes all disease-effect estimates exploratory. These results show that preprocessing choice can determine whether fractal group differences are detectable and should therefore be treated as part of the biomarker definition.

title: Identification of Kinome Biomarkers and Therapeutic Rescue in cGMP-Linked Retinal Degeneration
abstract: Inherited retinal degenerations, such as Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP) and Leber’s congenital amaurosis (LCA), are major causes of progressive and irreversible vision loss. The large number of genes associated with these disorders makes their clinical and molecular characterization difficult, while systemic biomarkers for disease progression or treatment response remain limited. These challenges were addressed by targeting cGMP-associated mechanisms shared by RP and LCA and integrating systemic biomarker profiling with retinal outcomes. Kinase activity analysis (kinome analysis) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells distinguished healthy and diseased states and captured therapy-associated signatures in rd10 mice treated with LP-CN03, a liposomal formulation of the cGMP analog CN03. This first systemic analysis in a therapeutically responsive animal model highlights kinome analysis as a potential translational readout. Given shared cGMP signaling in RP and AIPL1 -associated LCA, LP-CN03’s therapeutic potential was further evaluated in a new CRISPR-Cas9-generated Aipl1 ⁻/⁻ mouse model. Treatment with LP-CN03 preserved retinal structure and function, as shown by electroretinography, longitudinal optical coherence tomography, fundus imaging, optomotor testing, and photoreceptor-specific gene expression. Together, these findings provide independent in vivo evidence for the neuroprotective effect of LP-CN03 in both cGMP-related RP and LCA, also highlighting the translational value of kinome profiling. title: Mapping the brain-web morphology to characterise ageing and cognitive impairment
abstract: Ageing reshapes human brain anatomy across spatial scales, yet its geometrical organisation remains difficult to quantify. Here we introduce SHARP (Spectral Hierarchy Analysis, Reconstruction and Prediction), which transfers hierarchical cosmic-web classification to structural MRI, identifying knots, filaments, sheets and voids at four spectral levels and combining their morphology with higher-order spatial statistics and anatomical measurements. In CamCAN , selected filament- and sheet-associated features show opposing correlations with age and distinct associations with subcortical and ventricular volumes. To quantify their contribution, we compare SHARP with a neural-network baseline combining 36 regional anatomical measurements, total brain volume and sex. Adding cosmologically motivated descriptors reduces the mean absolute error of MRI-only age prediction from 6.04 to 4.71 years (22%) in CamCAN and from 4.57 to 4.07 years (11%) in OASIS-3 under participant-independent validation. Brain-web morphology with only brain volume and sex already achieves 5.12 years in CamCAN . For cognitive-status classification in OASIS-3, SHARP identifies 85% of Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR)-positive observations at 86% specificity, compared with 78% sensitivity for the anatomical baseline at matched empirical specificity. These results demonstrate that cosmological methods provide complementary geometrical information and measurable gains in characterising brain ageing and cognitive impairment.

title: Accessing Mesoscale Functional Organization from Standard Functional MRI Leveraging AI-Based Super-Resolution
abstract: Access to the fine-scale functional organization of the human brain is essential for understanding cognition and neurological disorders yet remains beyond the reach of conventional functional MRI (fMRI) because of its limited spatial resolution and contrast-to-noise ratio. To overcome this limitation, we developed f-LENNS (functional Localization Enhancement via Neural-Net-Sharpening), an artificial intelligence (AI)-based framework that enhances the effective spatial resolution of reconstructed fMRI magnitude images. The model was trained exclusively on high-resolution synthetic MRI data using extensive domain randomization and no adversarial or generative components. This approach enables robust out-of-the-box generalization (without retraining) to experimental datasets obtained with diverse acquisitions, while effectively curbing hallucination. Our experiments show that our publicly available model substantially improves the spatial fidelity of functional activation maps across multiple imaging paradigms and generalizes to a cohort of individuals with atypical brain function caused by amblyopia (lazy eye). F-LENNS consistently outperforms conventional resolution enhancement approaches, including interpolation-based upsampling and sharpening methods. These findings demonstrate that AI-driven super-resolution combined with domain randomization can overcome domain shifts arising from differences in MRI acquisition, enabling scalable, fine-scale functional brain mapping with widely available MRI hardware. Summary statement Precision functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) at the mesoscale is transforming our understanding of human brain functions by enabling the visualization of fine-grained functional organization in the human brain. Recent advances have shown that precision fMRI can reveal heterogeneous cortical architecture, resolve mesoscale processing streams underlying sensory perception, attention, and decision-making, identify functional alterations associated with neurological disorders, and help explain inter-individual variability in cognition. However, the widespread adoption of these approaches remains constrained by the limited availability of ultra-high-field MRI systems. Here, we introduce f-LENNS (functional Localization Enhancement via Neural-Net Sharpening), an artificial intelligence (AI)-based framework that broadens access to mesoscale functional neuroimaging by enhancing the effective spatial resolution of conventional fMRI. The model is trained exclusively on domain-randomized synthetic MRI data and generalizes to diverse datasets without retraining : f-LENNS can super-resolve data obtained with different acquisition parameters and at different magnetic field strengths (3T and 7T), while minimizing hallucination artifacts. F-LENNS substantially improves the detectability and spatial fidelity of fine-scale functional organization defined by stimulus-evoked activity and accurately recovers mesoscale functional patterns from conventional-resolution fMRI. Importantly, the same model generalizes to individuals with atypical brain function, revealing disorder-related functional abnormalities without data- or disease-specific retraining. Together, these findings demonstrate that domain randomization enables AI-based super-resolution models to overcome domain shifts arising from heterogeneous MRI hardware and acquisition protocols. Compared with conventional approaches, including interpolation-based upsampling, AFNI sharpening, and AI models trained on real functional and/or structural MRI data, f-LENNS consistently provides superior reconstruction of fine-scale functional organization. By enabling precision functional imaging in individual participants using widely available MRI systems, f-LENNS expands access to mesoscale brain mapping and represents an important step toward scalable, individualized functional neuroimaging and precision medicine.

title: Automated MRI-Based Segmentation of the Cranio-Cervical Venous System Using a Dedicated Deep Learning Pipeline
abstract: ABSTRACT PURPOSE To develop an automated magnetic resonance imaging based segmentation pipeline for the cranio-cervical venous system (CCVS), a complex anatomical network for which no dedicated segmentation tool is currently available. MATERIALS AND METHODS A retrospective single-center cohort of 194 contrast-enhanced cranio-cervical MRI examinations acquired between 2019 and 2024 was used. Manual reference segmentations were initially performed on 50 examinations using 3D Slicer. A nnU-Net v2-based segmentation model was then trained through an iterative process combining automatic segmentation, manual correction, and retraining. A dedicated intermediate model was developed to distinguish the vertebral artery from the surrounding vertebral venous plexus. Segmentation performance was assessed using the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC). The complete processing pipeline was integrated into an open-source software application, VenousNetworkAnalyzer (VNA). RESULTS The final model achieved a mean DSC of 0.94 (95% CI, 0.93–0.95) in five-fold cross-validation on 106 examinations with manual reference segmentations. Iterative optimization progressively reduced manual processing time from approximately 10 hours of fully manual segmentation to less than 10 minutes of manual correction per patient. Application of the final model to the entire cohort enabled the generation of patient-specific three-dimensional reconstructions of the cranio-cervical venous system. The segmentation workflow was successfully integrated into the VNA software environment, allowing automated processing and visualization of MRI datasets. CONCLUSION This study demonstrates the feasibility of automated segmentation of the cranio-cervical venous system from contrast-enhanced MRI using a dedicated deep-learning pipeline. The resulting reduction in processing time and integration into an open-source software platform provide a foundation for future large-scale anatomical studies of cranio-cervical venous drainage. Summary Statement An automated nnU-Net-based MRI pipeline enabled segmentation and three-dimensional visualization of the cranio-cervical venous system, reducing manual correction time less than 10 minutes per case. Key Points - A dedicated nnU-Net v2-based pipeline was developed for MRI-based segmentation of the cranio-cervical venous system - Iterative model optimization reduced manual processing time from approximately 10 hours to less than 10 minutes per case. - The pipeline enabled patient-specific three-dimensional reconstructions and was integrated into a dedicated software environment for visualization and analyzis.

title: MLX-Radiomics: accelerating standardized regional and voxel-wise radiomics for CT, PET and MRI
abstract: BackgroundDifferences among radiomics implementations complicate cross-study comparisons, while voxel-wise feature extraction remains computationally demanding. We developed MLX-Radiomics to accelerate regional feature extraction and voxel-wise mapping while preserving agreement with standardized reference measurements. MethodsMLX-Radiomics implements 172 feature definitions from the Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI), 16 extensions and the IBSI 2 image filters. We assessed agreement with IBSI reference data and evaluated numerical accuracy against independent double-precision and analytic calculations. In matched comparisons on Apple M1 Max and M5 Max systems, we used the IBSI reference CT to compare feature values, extraction time and memory use with PyRadiomics, MIRP and Flash-Radiomics, and feature values with FastRad. Separately, we compared the time required to generate voxel-wise feature maps for regions of up to 10.1 million voxels with published GPU results obtained on different hardware and images. We evaluated agreement with MIRP under published settings in a 51-patient cohort with CT, FDG PET and T1-weighted MRI. title: OmniT2I: a unified table-to-image framework for survival prediction and cross-modal inference with incomplete multimodal cancer data
abstract: Molecular profiles and histopathology provide complementary information about cancer prognosis, but these data are often incomplete for individual patients. Here we present OmniT2I, a table-to-image framework for survival prediction and cross-modal inference from incomplete multimodal cancer data. Each molecular profile was converted into a three-channel image representation with correlation-based feature placement. OmniT2I combines available molecular and histopathology embeddings through availability-aware fusion and predicts missing modalities from those observed. Across 10,373 patients with 32 cancer types, the C-index was 0.631 within cancer types and 0.783 with all cancers pooled (0.660 and 0.787 in 5,605 patients with all five modalities). A single model handled all 31 modality combinations and, compared with nine survival methods trained separately for each, achieved higher C-indices in 240 of 279 pooled and 226 of 279 within-cancer comparisons. Adding measured histopathology to RNA produced the largest within-cancer C-index gain among the four additional modalities evaluated, whereas adding copy number variation reduced it. In seven external cohorts, frozen RNA-only C-indices differed from test performance in the corresponding cancer type in TCGA by a median of −0.003 (range, −0.092 to +0.079). title: WALRUS: Robust and Transferable Deep Learning for Water and Lipid Removal in 1H-MRSI
abstract: Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging (1H-MRSI) enables non-invasive mapping of brain metabolism, but reliable quantification is challenged by residual water and extracranial lipid contamination. Recent work demonstrated that a deep learning model trained on simulated metabolite spectra combined with in vivo-derived water and lipid signals can outperform conventional nuisance-removal methods. However, this approach relied on heuristic simulation parameter distributions and a subject-specific L2-derived lipid estimate as an auxiliary network input, requiring subject-specific lipid masks and L2 processing during inference. Here, we introduce WALRUS (Water And Lipid Removal Using Spectral Learning), a fitting-consistent and empirically calibrated framework developed through a systematic evaluation of simulation realism, architectural priors, and network optimization. WALRUS uses the same metabolite basis as downstream spectral fitting and calibrates deliberately broadened simulation distributions from in vivo measurements. Controlled 7 T experiments demonstrate that empirical simulator calibration substantially improves nuisance removal and metabolite quantification compared with heuristic training distributions. With the optimized simulator, a capacity-matched comparison reveals no clear additional benefit from the L2-derived prior, allowing its removal and substantially simplifying inference. Further improvements are achieved with the final higher-capacity U-Net, while on-the-fly simulation improves generalization compared with training on a fixed synthetic dataset. The same framework was subsequently recalibrated and retrained at 3 T, where WALRUS outperformed conventional HLSVD+L2 processing on held-out data. Together, WALRUS combines these advances into an optimized framework that improves nuisance removal and downstream metabolite fitting, requires no subject-specific lipid segmentation or L2-derived auxiliary input during inference, and can be systematically adapted to different acquisition settings.

title: Large Language Models to Label CT Radiology Reports for Incidental Findings Found in Lung Cancer Screening: A Comparative Analysis
abstract: ObjectiveTo compare LLM and prompting strategies for labeling Specific Incidental Findings (SIFs) occurring during lung cancer screening, in radiology reports. Materials and MethodsIn this retrospective study, 300 CT reports from a Dutch academic hospital were included between 19th March 2003 and 28th December 2020. GPT-5, GPT-4-Turbo, Llama-3.1-8B-INST, MedGemma-4B-IT, a keyword-based search method, and a radiologist labelled the reports for the presence or absence of nine SIFs. The radiologists scores were the reference standard. Each LLM was evaluated with four different prompting strategies: two without Chain-of-Thought (CoT), and two with CoT (one zero shot, one few shot). The automated labelling methods were evaluated against the radiologist primarily using Cohens Kappa, and additionally sensitivity, specificity, and F1 scores. ResultsGPT-5 achieved substantial or almost perfect agreement for seven out of nine SIFs: aortic valve disease, bronchiectasis, consolidation, coronary artery calcification, emphysema, abnormality in mediastinal lymph nodes, and thyroid abnormalities, with Cohen {kappa} values of 0.81 (0.70, 0.93), 0.97 (0.93, 1.00), 0.71 (0.62, 0.82), 0.92 (0.87, 0.96), 0.91 (0.84, 0.97), 0.71 (0.62, 0.80), and 0.92 (0.86, 0.98) respectively. For the remaining two SIFs, moderate LLM agreement was obtained with MedGemma-4B-IT and with GPT-4-Turbo with Cohen {kappa} values of 0.48 (0.40, 0.60), 0.42 (0.31, 0.58) for interstitial lung abnormalities and mediastinal mass respectively. The highest agreement was obtained with the non-CoT prompt strategies for most SIFs. ConclusionThis study demonstrated that LLMs can automatically label radiology reports with agreement ranging from almost perfect to moderate, but not one LLM - prompt combination achieved the highest agreement across all SIFs.

title: Cortical brain changes from early to mid-adolescence in offspring at familial high risk for schizophrenia or bipolar disorder
abstract: Objective: Schizophrenia (SZ) and bipolar disorder (BP) emerge in late adolescence or adulthood. Offspring at familial high risk for SZ (FHR-SZ) or BP (FHR-BP) are more likely to develop psychiatric disorders. Prior work from the Danish High Risk and Resilience (VIA) Study found sex-specific volumetric brain differences in offspring at FHR-SZ and FHR-BP aged 11-12 years. This study builds upon these findings by testing whether they reflect group differences in rate of change or stable group differences from early to mid-adolescence. Methods: This study investigated MRI data from offspring at FHR-SZ, FHR-BP, and population- based controls (PBC) at baseline (11-12 years; n=288) and follow-up (15-16 years; n=249). FreeSurfer longitudinal processing derived total brain volume, cortical measures, and intracranial volume (ICV). Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-age interactions and sex-specific group effects, as well as associations with psychotic experiences (PE) and lifetime Axis-I mental disorders. Results: The analysis did not detect group-by-age interactions, indicating similar developmental slopes across groups. However, at both time points, males at FHR-SZ demonstrated reduced brain and cortical volumes compared to PBC and FHR-BP males. These effects were attenuated after adjusting for ICV, which was reduced in males at FHR-SZ. The analysis additionally detected volumetric reductions in males with PE, after controlling for risk status. Conclusions: These results extend the previous findings to ages 15-16 years, indicating group differences are stable and persist into mid-adolescence. Associations with ICV suggest early neurodevelopmental effects, and volumetric reductions in males with PE suggest convergent effects with FHR-SZ.

title: Lamina Cribrosa Strain as a Glaucoma Prognostic Factor: The STRAIN Study Methodology and Initial Outcomes
abstract: Objective To estimate the lamina cribrosa (LC) strain response to intraocular pressure (IOP) change in open angle glaucoma (OAG) patients and examine associations between LC strain and demographic and clinical characteristics relevant to OAG in an ongoing longitudinal study. Design Cohort study Participants Adult patients with OAG (205 eyes of 119 patients) Methods The STRAIN study is an ongoing longitudinal study designed to determine whether LC biomechanical strain is associated with present, prior, and future OAG damage. In this initial analysis, patients either temporarily stopped ≥1 eye drop, initiated an eye drop, or underwent selective laser trabeculoplasty to produce IOP change. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans of the optic nerve head (ONH) acquired before and up to several weeks after IOP change were analyzed using digital volume correlation (DVC) to estimate LC strain. Strain measurements were compared with age, race, sex, axial length, central corneal thickness (CCT), corneal hysteresis, optic disc area, years of known OAG, retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness, and visual field mean deviation (MD). Main Outcome Measures LC strain estimated by DVC from OCT scans acquired before and after IOP alteration. Results Axial LC strain ( Ezz ) was tensile with IOP decrease and compressive with IOP increase. Maximum principal strain was tensile (mean E max = 1.09%), and maximum shear strain was positive (mean Γ max = 1.16%) in the radial-axial plane. Both increased quadratically with the IOP change. Older age was significantly related to greater tensile circumferential strain ( p = 0.02) and lower Γ max ( p = 0.01). Sex, CCT, corneal hysteresis, and optic disc area were not significantly associated with LC strain. In combined multivariable models adjusting for IOP change, demographics, and accounting for correlations between eyes from the same patient, eyes with thinner inferior-quadrant RNFL had smaller Γ max for a given IOP change ( p = 0.02). Conclusions LC strain in patients with OAG is associated with the degree of neuronal loss, age, and axial length, supporting a relationship between the LC biomechanical response and factors relevant to glaucomatous damage.

title: LungAI: An AI Biomarker that Refines Lung-RADS v2022 Triage of Screen-Detected Pulmonary Nodules
abstract: BackgroundThe Lung-RADS algorithm standardizes the management of screen-detected pulmonary nodules, but its risk assessment is driven chiefly by nodule size and attenuation. This misallocates a meaningful fraction of patients: a nontrivial share of small malignancies receive 12-month surveillance while large benign nodules proceed to invasive workup. Artificial intelligence (AI) may supply risk information independent of the imaging features Lung-RADS already uses. MethodsWe validated LungAI, an investigational deep learning nodule malignancy classifier not yet cleared by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), on the held-out NLST test partition of Ardila et al. (2,747 low-dose CT examinations from 1,244 patients with [≥]1 solid or part-solid 4-30 mm nodule; 89 pathologically confirmed cancers, prevalence 3.2%). We compared discrimination against Sybil, mean nodule diameter, and estimated nodule volume. A board-certified radiologist assigned Lung-RADS v2022 categories to a positives-enriched random subset (226 eligible examinations; 78 cancers), projected to the full cohort by contingency weighting. A per-category reclassification algorithm shifted patients along the existing Lung-RADS management ladder using a-priori score cutpoints. We evaluated a separately locked follow-up configuration on examinations with a prior scan. ResultsLungAI achieved AUROC 0.92 (95% CI 0.88-0.95) and AUPRC 0.47 (0.35-0.61), outperforming Sybil ({Delta}AUROC 0.07; {Delta}AUPRC 0.18), diameter ({Delta}AUROC 0.14; {Delta}AUPRC 0.34), and volume ({Delta}AUROC 0.14; {Delta}AUPRC 0.38; all P<0.001). title: Beyond organ age gaps: comparing plasma proteomic metrics of organ biology in relation to brain structure and neurodegenerative disease
abstract: Biological aging is heterogeneous across organ systems, and brain health may be influenced by biological processes extending beyond the central nervous system (CNS). This can be investigated using biological age measures that are increasingly used to estimate how biological systems deviate from chronological aging. However, organ level plasma proteomic metrics may capture different forms of biological variation depending on how they are defined. Here, we compared three complementary organ level proteomic metrics across 15 organ systems (and two global systems) in relation to age, organ-relevant physiological phenotypes, brain morphometry, and incident neurodegenerative disease, using plasma proteomics from 52,667 UK Biobank participants and brain MRI data from 5,078 of those individuals. We derived i) supervised age gap metrics using XGBoost models trained to predict chronological age, ii) unsupervised PC1 metrics capturing dominant organ-associated proteomic variation, and iii) phenotype guided PLS metrics linking plasma proteins to organ-relevant physiological traits. The three metric classes were related but not interchangeable. Global all-protein and all-organ-protein models showed strong age-related proteomic structure. However, organ-specific PC analyses showed that age was often but not always the dominant source of variation in protein signal across organs. Age gap metrics showed the most consistent associations with subsequent ICD-10based neurodegenerative and vascular diagnoses, whereas all three metric classes showed distinct associations with brain structure and organ-relevant physiological phenotypes. Brain structure analyses revealed heterogeneous organ–brain association patterns across organs, suggesting that proteomic variation relates to brain structure in both a systemic and an organ-specific manner. Several systemic and organ-specific signals partially mediated the associations between disease specific genetic risk and incident diagnoses of Alzheimer’s disease and stroke, albeit with small effect sizes (1-8%). Similarly, organ metrics provided modest incremental predictive improvement over baseline demographic models, with the largest increase in ROC-AUC observed for Alzheimer’s disease when all organ age gap metrics were added jointly (ΔROC-AUC = 0.037). These results link brain related outcomes to proteomic variation across both CNS and non-CNS systems. Our work suggests that proteomic organ metrics capture complementary dimensions of biological variation rather than a single construct of organ aging. Although these measures may provide informative biological and potentially predictive signals, their incremental predictive value in the present analyses was modest.

title: Volumetric Analysis of the Deltoid Muscle From Neck-to-Knee Dixon MRI: A pilot population assessment of a posterior intramuscular injection target
abstract: BackgroundDeltoid muscle volume varies across anatomical regions and population groups, with potential implications for intramuscular injection site selection. Evidence comparing middle and posterior deltoid volumes in vaccine-eligible populations is limited. PurposeTo compare middle and posterior deltoid muscle volumes by vaccine eligibility group, sex, and side. MethodsDeltoid muscles were manually segmented into anterior, middle and posterior regions in 43 UK Biobank Dixon MRI scans. A MONAI deep learning model trained on the annotations (Dice score = 0.78) segmented deltoid muscles of 5,239 participants, categorised by UK flu vaccination eligibility: A ([≥]65 years without risk conditions, n=1,760), B ([≥]65 with risk conditions, n=1,744), and C (<65 with risk conditions, n=1,735). Bilateral-average posterior and middle volumes were compared using a paired t-test. A linear mixed-effects model assessed posterior-middle differences by group, sex and side. ResultsMean age was 66.7 {+/-} 7.2 years and body mass index was 27.5 {+/-} 5.7 kg/m2 (mean {+/-} SD). Posterior deltoid volume exceeded the middle deltoid volume by 55.36 ml (95% CI, 54.14-56.58, p<0.0001). Posterior-middle differences were largest in Group A, followed by B and then C, greater in men, and greater on the right side (all p<0.0001). Mean segmentation-quality score was 4.27 {+/-} 0.73 on a five-point Likert scale and weighted inter-observer kappa was 0.583 (95% CI, 0.452 - 0.713). ConclusionsAmong individuals eligible for the UK flu immunisation, posterior deltoid volume was greater than middle deltoid volume. These findings support further anatomical assessment of the posterior deltoid as a potentially safer injection target. Key ResultsO_LIThe deltoid muscles of 5,239 participants from the UK Biobank matching UK annual influenza vaccination eligibility were segmented using a deep learning-based model, enabling precise volumetric quantification of the anterior, middle and posterior deltoids. C_LIO_LIThese findings provide a comprehensive reference framework for deltoid assessment across different ages and genders, enhancing both research and clinical decision-making for IM injection site selection. C_LI Summary statementAutomated deltoid volumetry in a pilot UK Biobank cohort revealed greater posterior than middle deltoid volume, supporting further evaluation of the posterior deltoid for a potential alternative intramuscular vaccination site.

title: Silent Drift and Site-level Variance in Clinical AI: Real-world performance and subgroup analysis for post-market monitoring of an FDA-cleared artificial intelligence (AI) triage tool for high-risk use case of pulmonary embolism
abstract: BackgroundFDA-cleared artificial intelligence (AI) triage tool for pulmonary embolism (PE) detection has been widely used; however, its performance has not been analyzed for subgroups, clinical sites, and temporal stability. MethodsThis retrospective, six-site health system study evaluated the Aidoc BriefCase PE triage model (K190072) across 14,736 CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) examinations between July 2023 and March 2026. Reference-standard PE characteristic labels were extracted from radiology reports using a zero-shot LLM pipeline validated against a radiologist-annotated 600 reports ({kappa} =0.98). Model performance was evaluated across demographics, embolus characteristics, and site. title: Deep Learning Identifies BMI-Associated Morphologic Features in Breast Cancer Tissue
abstract: A bstract Multiple epidemiological studies have established obesity as an adverse factor in breast cancer incidence, progression, and clinical outcomes. However, the biological mechanisms underlying these associations remain incompletely understood. In peritumoral adipose tissue, obesity is associated with chronic inflammation, macrophage recruitment, and broader alterations in the local microenvironment. Whether these obesity-associated changes are accompanied by distinct morphologic features within the tumor and non-adipose stromal compartments remains unclear. In this study, we investigated whether an AI-based pathology foundation model could support the development of machine learning algorithms capable of identifying obesity-associated morphologic patterns in histopathology images, with a particular focus on tumor and stromal regions. In a cohort of 195 patients with breast cancer, machine learning models using vector embeddings from non-adipose stromal regions classified high BMI (≥30 kg/m 2 ) versus low BMI (<25 kg/m 2 ) with an average AUC of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.73–0.83), consistently outperforming models based on tumor-only or combined tumor–stroma regions. These obesity-associated stromal signatures were observed across subgroups defined by hormone-receptor status and age, indicating that they are not restricted to specific clinical populations. Complementary embedding-based dissimilarity analysis further showed that higher BMI was associated with reduced inter-patient heterogeneity in both tumor and stromal tissues. Overall, these findings suggest that obesity is associated with distinct morphologic alterations in both tumor and non-adipose stromal tissues. Notably, the stromal compartment emerged as a particularly informative indicator of obesity-associated morphology and demonstrated reduced inter-patient heterogeneity among individuals with high BMI.

title: A Multi-Cohort nnU-Net for White Matter Hyperintensity Segmentation Across 2D and 3D FLAIR Acquisitions
abstract: ABSTRACT Background White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are increasingly pooled across aging, cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD), and dementia cohorts that differ in both disease composition and FLAIR acquisition. Most automated segmentation tools were developed within a narrower range of populations or protocols, and few have been tested for whether segmentation accuracy and error remain consistent across conventional 2D and isotropic 3D FLAIR, or whether the choice of algorithm alters downstream clinical associations. Methods We developed a single nnU-Net model, taking FLAIR and T1-weighted images as inputs, using 460 2D and 3D FLAIR scans from a neurodegenerative cohort (Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, ADNI), a CSVD-enriched cohort with same-visit paired 2D and 3D FLAIR (Washington University White Matter Ischemic-Hypoxia study, WWISH), and a population-based sample (UK Biobank), holding out 92 scans from 66 participants at the participant-level as an internal test set. We further evaluated the model in an independent ADNI3 3D FLAIR set (n = 25), benchmarking voxel-wise overlap (Dice), volumetric agreement, and lesion-level detection against SHIVA-WMH, segcsvdWMH, and FreeSurfer WMH-SynthSeg, and compared acquisition-specific volume bias in participants with paired 2D and 3D FLAIR. We then compared how WMH volumes from each method predicted incident dementia in cognitively unimpaired adults from ADNI and the Knight Alzheimer Disease Research Center (n = 1,174; 42 incident cases). Results In the internal test set, the model achieved a mean Dice of 0.73 (SD 0.10), compared with 0.50, 0.57, and 0.29 for SHIVA-WMH, segcsvdWMH, and WMH-SynthSeg (all FDR-adjusted p < 0.001). Dice was similar on 2D and 3D FLAIR (0.75 vs. 0.71). In WWISH participants imaged with both acquisitions, mean volume bias differed between 2D and 3D scans by 1.8 mL for the model versus 4.7–9.9 mL for the comparators. Advantages were largest in low-burden scans (<5 mL; Dice 0.66 vs. 0.19–0.54) and for lesions of ≤100 voxels (detection 77–87% vs. 14–63%). In ADNI3, the model retained a mean Dice of 0.70 (SD 0.14) without retraining and exceeded all comparators (FDR-adjusted p ≤ 0.002). Model-derived WMH volume was associated with incident dementia beyond clinical covariates (OR per SD 1.40, 95% CI 1.11–1.77; likelihood-ratio p = 0.009; cross-validated AUC 0.71 vs. 0.68), whereas comparator-derived volumes did not significantly improve model fit. Conclusions Training a single model across disease contexts and FLAIR acquisitions yielded WMH segmentation that was similarly accurate on 2D and 3D FLAIR, sensitive to low-burden disease, transferable to an unseen protocol, and clinically informative, supporting its use in multi-cohort, mixed-etiology studies. KEY POINTS A single nnU-Net trained across neurodegenerative, cerebral small vessel disease, and population-based cohorts and across 2D and 3D FLAIR outperformed SHIVA-WMH, segcsvdWMH, and WMH-SynthSeg, with the largest gains in low-burden scans and small lesions. In same-visit paired 2D and 3D FLAIR scans, the model’s volume bias relative to acquisition-specific reference masks varied less across acquisitions, whereas comparator biases varied with acquisition. Only WMH volume from the model significantly improved model fit for incident dementia beyond clinical covariates, highlighting the potential influence of segmentation algorithm choice on downstream clinical inference.

title: Reliability-Aware Clinical Relation Learning for Uncertainty-Robust Multi-Label Chest X-ray Classification
abstract: Background Automated multi-label classification of chest radiographs is complicated by overlapping imaging findings, noisy report-derived labels, and changes in disease co-occurrence across clinical settings. Existing clinical-hierarchy methods can encode label relationships, but a rigid hierarchy may conflate categorical membership with empirical association and propagate annotation errors. Methods We investigated Reliability-Aware Clinical Relation Learning (ReCaRL), a graph-assisted framework for multi-label chest radiograph classification. An image encoder produces initial finding scores, while a graph constructed from training-label associations provides reliability-weighted, confidence-gated updates. Uncertain annotations are handled with observation masks. The evaluation compares flat, weighted, graph-based, and hierarchy-penalty baselines, with internal and external discrimination and calibration assessments. Results In the internal evaluation, ReCaRL achieved macro AUROC 0.821 and macro AUPRC 0.437, compared with 0.812 and 0.423 for the masked/weighted baseline. Mean AUROC across five common findings was 0.865 versus 0.858. External testing yielded AUROC 0.799 and AUPRC 0.409. Post-hoc calibration reduced the internal Brier score from 0.113 to 0.102 and the external expected calibration error from 0.082 to 0.061, without changing AUROC or AUPRC. Conclusions Reliability-aware graph propagation and confidence gating were associated with modest improvements in multi-label chest radiograph classification relative to the matched masked/weighted baseline. Post-hoc calibration improved probability reliability in the reported evaluations. The findings do not establish a benefit in prospective clinical decision-making.

title: Artificial intelligence for pulmonary tuberculosis detection on chest X-ray images: A systematic review and diagnostic accuracy meta-analysis
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based computer-aided detection (CAD) of tuberculosis (TB) on chest X-ray (CXR) may standardize screening and triage in settings with few radiologists but its accuracy in clinical cohorts remains uncertain. We searched five databases (PubMed, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, OpenAlex, Lens.org) on 15 March 2026 for studies published between January 2020 and March 2026, and we appraised these studies using QUADAS-2. Evaluations from clinical cohorts with complete 2 x 2 data and a microbiological or composite reference standard for all participants were pooled using a bivariate random-effects model, with 95% prediction intervals. We accounted for overlapping participants by performing a post hoc analysis with one evaluation per cohort and used GRADE to assess the certainty of the evidence. No protocol was prepared or registered. We included 21 studies (26 evaluations of AI models). Nine evaluations from three independent cohorts were pooled. Pooled sensitivity was 0.896 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.874 to 0.915, prediction interval 0.798 to 0.950) and pooled specificity was 0.689 (95% CI 0.642 to 0.732; prediction interval 0.499 to 0.831). Both confidence intervals include the World Health Organization (WHO) triage thresholds (sensitivity 90%, specificity 70%). When a screening study with partial verification was added, pooled specificity increased to 0.735. Eighteen of 24 assessed evaluations were at high risk of bias and only 1 of 21 studies was prospective, fully verified, externally validated and met the WHO thresholds. Certainty of evidence was low for sensitivity and very low for specificity. A subsequent PubMed search found additional eligible clinical evaluations that were not screened, so the review is incomplete for those studies. In clinical cohorts, AI-CXR sensitivity is close to the WHO triage target, and specificity is close to, but not clearly above, its target. The evidence is pooled across only three cohorts, and specificity varies by product and setting. Thresholds need to be calibrated locally, and prospective, externally validated evaluations are needed before widespread deployment.

title: Circular-Arc Modal Migration for Ultrasound Imaging—Part I: Finite-Arc Spectral Theory and Stolt–Pullback Factorization
abstract: Circular-arc ultrasound imaging requires a spectral construction that accommodates radius-dependent propagation and the spatially varying phase of offset-source transmission. This first of two articles develops Circular-Arc Modal Migration (CAMM), a direct Stolt-type imaging framework in angular modal coordinates. Starting from a first-Born acoustic model, angular decomposition and local radial Stolt mappings convert channel spectra into fields for coherent image synthesis. The offset transmit phase is represented by a phase-screen factorization through reusable spectral factors and spatially weighted fields. A scalar-pullback approximation simplifies this correction to reading one reference image at a geometrically fitted radial coordinate. Both realizations share the same modal construction. Error controls address local radial synthesis, transmit-path expansion, scalar approximation, and phase-screen truncation, with direct integration verifying the separated numerical evaluation. Same-RF point-target comparisons show that scalar pullback closely preserves the principal peak positions and widths of phase-screen imaging in the compact semicircular configuration, while phase screens better control surrounding responses in the shallow convex examples. The retained modal spectrum, frequency band, image radius, and source displacement guide this accuracy–computation choice. CAMM thereby extends direct spectral image formation to circular arcs and supplies the theoretical and numerical basis for the image-quality and performance studies in Part II.

title: Anatomy-preserving rare-subregion correction for pediatric brain tumor segmentation on multiparametric MRI: a BraTS-PEDs 2026 challenge study
abstract: Pediatric brain tumor subregion segmentation is strongly imbalanced: whole-tumor anatomy is comparatively stable, whereas enhancing tumor (ET), cystic component (CC), and edema (ED) may be absent or small. We present an anatomy-preserving multi-stage system for BraTS-PEDs 2026 Task 2. A five-fold residual-encoder nnU-Net supplies robust anatomy and calibrated out-of-fold priors. Candidate ET and CC regions are recovered by independent fold agreement and component-level filters. A rare-aware residual adapter then operates only inside voxels labeled non-enhancing tumor core (NETC), using MRI, signed intermodality contrasts, probability uncertainty, spatial anatomy, and coordinates. Its constrained assembly permits only NETC-to-ET or NETC-to-CC transitions; therefore background, ED, tumor core, and whole tumor are invariant. On 236 out-of-fold cases, the adapter improved CC Dice from 0.223 to 0.253 and CC normalized surface Dice from 0.233 to 0.263, while preserving tumor-core and whole-tumor scores exactly. The frozen Docker submission achieved Dice scores of 0.510, 0.908, 0.144, 0.000, 0.937, and 0.937 for ET, NETC, CC, ED, tumor core, and whole tumor, respectively, on the 91-case challenge validation set. The results show that constrained rare-subtype correction can improve difficult labels without sacrificing strong anatomical predictions, while also exposing persistent domain shift for CC and ED.

title: TRACE: Trajectory Reconstruction and Clustering from Sparse Evidence for Disease Subtyping and Staging
abstract: A bstract Chronic progressive diseases often follow heterogeneous courses, with individuals differing in the pattern and timing of biomarker abnormalities. However, observed data are typically sparse and predominantly cross-sectional, with limited follow-up covering only short segments of disease progression. Reconstructing heterogeneous trajectories from such data requires disentangling variation along disease trajectories from subtype heterogeneity while inferring individuals’ unknown sub-type assignments and disease stages. Existing approaches may confound disease stage with subtype, scale poorly as the number of biomarkers increases, or fail to effectively integrate cross-sectional and longitudinal observations. We propose TRACE ( T rajectory R econstruction A nd C lustering from Sparse E vidence), a probabilistic framework that jointly reconstructs biomarker trajectories and infers disease subtypes and continuous stages. TRACE combines monotonic neural networks for flexible modeling and data-driven clustering of subtype-specific progression trajectories with temporal regularization derived from longitudinal observations when available. All model components are jointly optimized end to end using stochastic gradient descent, enabling efficient and scalable estimation. We evaluate TRACE on semi-simulated MRI biomarker data with known subtype and stage structures and demonstrate its ability to identify clinically meaningful subtypes and disease stages in real-world neurodegenerative disease datasets.

title: Anatomy-Aware 3D GAN with Local Mask Refinement for Brain MRI Inpainting
abstract: Brain tumor MRI inpainting aims to synthesize plausible healthy-appearing tissue in regions removed from pathological scans. We present an anatomy-aware three-dimensional generative adversarial network for Task 4 of the BraTS 2026 challenge. The method combines mask-aware gated convolutions, mirrored contralateral context, attention-modulated skip fusion, boundary-aware refinement, and a local masked-region refiner, each adapted from established components in the image synthesis and inpainting literature. The model is trained with a two-stage objective that first emphasizes voxel-wise and structural reconstruction and then applies low-weight adversarial fine-tuning. On a deterministic local held-out split, the proposed method substantially improves over a simple 3D AutoEncoder baseline but does not surpass the challenges Pix2Pix3D baseline. On the official BraTS 2026 Task 4 evaluation server, the submitted model obtained a mean SSIM of 0.658 and a mean PSNR of 14.81 dB over 219 evaluated cases, lower than the local held-out figures. We report these results transparently, analyze likely contributing factors, and identify the controlled ablations (removal of the mirrored-context channel and of the two-stage schedule) required to isolate the contribution of each architectural component.

abstract: PurposeTo develop and validate a fully automated pipeline that measures skeletal muscle and adipose tissue at L1 and L3 on routine CT with varied scan ranges, slice orders and contrast phases, rejects levels outside the scan and converts measures to non-contrast equivalents. We evaluated it on five single-centre datasets (4986 series): agreement with radiologist-corrected labels using five-fold cross-fitting (2025 series), artificially truncated scans, contrast-enhanced series paired with non-contrast series of the same examination, and the prognostic value of fully automated measures in 2006 patients after curative cancer surgery. title: Segment Anything for Microscopy 2
abstract: Foundation models have advanced microscopy image segmentation, but existing models are trained on two-dimensional data, struggle with complex structures in volumetric data, and address only a narrow range of analysis tasks. Here we present Segment Anything for Microscopy 2 (μSAM2), a foundation model that adapts SAM2 to joint 2D and 3D segmentation in light and electron microscopy. Trained on annotations of more than 23 million cells and nuclei and 1.6 million cellular structures, μSAM2 achieves state-of-the-art automatic and interactive segmentation and outperforms generalist and specialist methods on volumetric data. Dedicated models further enable accurate mitochondrion and nucleus segmentation in electron microscopy. Beyond segmentation, μSAM2 supports pixel and object classification from few annotations as well as cell tracking in 2D and 3D time-lapse data. All functionality is available in the user-friendly μSAM napari plugin. We demonstrated the capabilities of μSAM2 on challenging use cases spanning developmental biology, organoid research, cardiac physiology, and histopathology.

title: Restoring Marčenko-Pastur noise estimation and denoising of diffusion MRI under common image reconstruction
abstract: Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging can reveal microstructure in the living brain, but the measurements are inherently noisy. Marčenko–Pastur denoising is a widely used remedy, helping to separate signal from noise under a simplified noise covariance model. However, we find that the model breaks under common image reconstructions across 28 public in vivo datasets, resulting in weaker denoising than intended. We restore the intended denoising behavior with a noise covariance model estimated from the reconstructed images, and validate the estimated model on repeated ex vivo and in vivo scans. The method requires no additional measurements or knowledge of the reconstruction, opening headroom for microstructure analyses in both existing and newly acquired data.

title: Cortical surface area is an independent predictor of incident dementia
abstract: Cortical surface area (cSA) is associated with intelligence and cognition, yet structural MRI studies of neurodegeneration in Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD) have emphasized quantification of cortical thickness (cTH) and volume, with very limited evaluation of cSA. We examined whether cSA of AD-relevant brain regions provide diagnostic, prognostic, and biological information beyond cTH and volume across 5,430 participants (3,124 cognitively unimpaired; 1,634 mild cognitive impairment [MCI]; 672 ADRD) from three aging and dementia cohorts: the National Alzheimer’s Coordinating Center, Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, and Carotids and Minds study. In cross-sectional analyses, cSA and cTH showed weak correlation, and lower cSA was independently associated with greater odds of MCI and ADRD after adjustment for cTH and covariates. Participants with both low cSA and low cTH had greater risk of MCI and ADRD compared to low cSA, cTH, or volume alone. In longitudinal models, baseline cSA predicted incident ADRD independent from cTH, and combined cSA/cTH models outperformed cSA, cTH, or volume alone for predicting incident ADRD over a mean follow-up of 4.3 years. Complementing these findings, proteomics analyses revealed distinct signatures associated with cSA compared to cTH. Overall, these findings support cSA as a clinically informative and biologically distinct dimension of AD-related cortical vulnerability.

title: MeXalign – A Segmentation Mask-Based Registration Pipeline for Multimodal Single-Cell Analysis
abstract: Leveraging the power of multimodal imaging relies on accurate coregistration of yet fundamentally different modalities. Reliable cell-to-cell correspondence is especially challenging as consecutive tissue sections do not necessarily contain identical cells or cellular structures. Here we present MeXalign, a segmentation-mask-based coregistration pipeline designed to integrate multimodal images acquired sequentially from the same specimen at single-cell resolution. Single-cell segmentation masks provide a modality-independent representation of cellular morphology and spatial organization. MeXalign was tested based on the two platforms, laser ablation inductively coupled plasma time-of-flight mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-TOFMS) and immunofluorescence (IF) microscopy. As a prerequisite, each modality integrates membrane and/or nucleus labels for accurate segmentation. The added value of MeXalign was highlighted for imaging of cell models deposited on glass slides and tissue sections. The performance of coregistration was validated on cytospins, murine tumor and human skin samples. A dedicated scoring system was introduced allowing to assess the quality of image coregistration. The robustness towards under-segmentation and downstream image analysis was evaluated on LA-ICP-TOFMS with and without coregistration, investigating metal drug uptake, barcoding and cellular phenotyping. A showcase study on cancer cells exposed to nanoparticles proved the accuracy, as the nanoparticle distribution was preserved at a subcellular level when using MeXalign. While all examples show the overall improved quality of segmentation, other benefits of complementary labelings can be anticipated, especially for cellular features unique to one modality. title: MR-based normative volumetric analyses reveal genotype-dependent brain anomalies in FGFR -related craniosynostoses
abstract: Craniostenosis, a cranial malformation due to premature suture fusion, includes rare FGFR -related conditions such as Crouzon (CS), Muenke (MS), and Apert (AS) syndromes. These mutations affect skull but also brain development and are associated with variable neurodevelopmental outcomes. This brain impairment is still poorly described and understood, prompting for neuroimaging anatomical studies. We thus investigated regional brain growth and volumetric scaling in patients with these three syndromes and non-syndromic non- FGFR -related craniostenoses, using a normative modelling framework. We analyzed a rare set of brain MRI from 65 patients close to first cranial surgery time (30 CS among which 23 pre-surgery, 4 AS, 6 MS, 23 non-syndromic) and 130 typically developing controls. Millimetric 3D T1-weighted images were segmented into 6 cortical and 3 subcortical regions (AssemblyNet, Morphologist). After harmonization (ComBat), normative growth curves (Turner model) and static scaling curves (power-law model, effect of brain size regardless of age) were derived in controls. Patient deviations were assessed using permutation tests on mean normalized distance to typical model and abnormality rates (10th/90th percentiles). Patients with CS showed typical brain volumes for age except for enlarged ventricles, but slightly overscaled frontal volumes for brain size. Non-syndromic patients showed very similar volume distribution for age and brain size than CS ones. Patients with AS displayed increased total brain, temporal, cerebellar and central volumes for age, with overscaled temporal and cerebellar regions but underscaled frontal volumes for brain size. Patients with MS showed a similar, though milder, pattern: increased temporal volume for age, with temporal overscaling but frontal underscaling for frain size. Our findings reveal genotype-dependent brain anomalies in FGFR -related craniosynostoses, with a convergent pattern of temporal–frontal disproportions in AS and MS, associated with very specific mutations in the FGFR2 and 3 genes respectively, contrasting with a much more typical brain organization in more heterogeneous CS and non-syndromic patients. Beyond the pathophysiological meaning of these results, which call for a larger similar study covering as wide a range of patient variability as possible, our work highlights the relevance of normative modelling approach for characterizing rare craniofacial disorders using clinical MRI datasets.

title: Normative Modeling of Structural and Diffusion MRI for Epilepsy Diagnosis and Classification
abstract: Background: and Objectives: Normative modeling expresses an individual's brain measures as deviations from a large healthy reference and has been advanced as a route to precision imaging biomarkers in epilepsy, where structural abnormality is distributed rather than confined to the presumed focus. Whether this framework can inform clinical classification from clinically acquired T1-weighted and diffusion MRI is untested. We asked whether normative deviations discriminate between (1) epilepsy and functional seizures; (2) focal and generalized epilepsy; and (3) drug-resistant and drug-responsive epilepsy. Methods: We retrospectively studied patients with epilepsy or functional seizures without comorbid epilepsy who underwent 3-Tesla epilepsy-protocol MRI at the University of Pennsylvania. Morphometric deviation scores (cortical thickness, subcortical volume) were derived from CentileBrain (n>37,000 healthy references). White matter fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity profiles were referenced to harmonized Human Connectome Project cohorts. Lobar composites, hemispheric asymmetry indices, and whole-tract means were compared with rank-sum tests; discrimination was summarized as area under the ROC curve (AUC) with bootstrap confidence intervals and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Whole-brain deviation burden was examined as a secondary analysis. Minimum detectable effects were estimated by Monte Carlo simulation at 80% power (α=0.05). Results: We included 273 patients with epilepsy (203 focal, 37 generalized, 33 unclassified; 97 drug-resistant, 176 drug-responsive) and 32 with functional seizures. In the primary analyses, no regional or tract-level normative measure distinguished epilepsy from functional seizures, focal from generalized epilepsy, or drug-resistant from drug-responsive epilepsy; AUCs did not exceed 0.62, with upper confidence limits up to 0.72. In the secondary analysis, whole-brain morphometric deviation burden was modestly higher in epilepsy than in functional seizures (AUC 0.66, 95% CI 0.57-0.74) but did not separate the within-epilepsy comparisons. The study could detect AUC ≥0.65 for epilepsy versus functional seizures, ≥0.64 for focal versus generalized, and ≥0.60 for drug-resistant versus drug-responsive epilepsy. Discussion: Univariate normative deviation summaries from clinical MRI do not currently distinguish these groups well enough to guide care. Whole-brain deviation burden, the only summary measure that differed after correction, was detectable at the group level but insufficient for individual-level classification. Progress may require network-targeted analysis of patient-specific deviations and multimodal integration.

title: Integrating Histopathology Foundation Models and PRAME Immunohistochemistry in Melanoma Diagnosis
abstract: Background: The histopathological diagnosis of challenging melanocytic lesions remains limited by substantial interobserver variability. Although computational pathology foundation models demonstrated promising diagnostic performance, their predictions are often difficult to interpret in terms of established criteria. Objective: We evaluated a diagnostic framework combining foundation-model-based whole-slide image analysis, automated prediction of morphological features, and manually assessed PRAME immunohistochemistry. Methods: Using the Virchow2 foundation model and STAMP framework, we analyzed a retrospective cohort of 1,000 melanocytic lesions undergoing PRAME immunohistochemistry. Models were trained on 800 cases and evaluated on a temporally held-out test cohort of 200 cases. Results: The slide-level malignancy classifier achieved a test AUROC of 0.970 (AUPRC 0.984). Separate models predicted established histopathological criteria with high discrimination, including ulceration (AUROC 0.991) and dermal mitoses (AUROC 0.966). In contrast, predicting PRAME expression from H&E images alone showed lower performance (AUROC 0.776-0.780 for PRAME scores 4 and 0). An integrated model combining the slide-level malignancy score, AI-predicted morphological features, and manual PRAME status achieved an AUROC of 0.972 (AUPRC 0.975), comparable to the standalone classifier. In multivariable analysis, PRAME score 4 versus 0 was strongly associated with malignancy (adjusted OR 35.04, 95% CI 17.39-74.62). Conclusions: These findings demonstrate the feasibility of combining foundation-model-based histopathological analysis with established morphological criteria and PRAME immunohistochemistry. Although the integrated framework did not substantially improve overall discrimination, it provides a structured approach for incorporating complementary histopathological and immunohistochemical information into AI-assisted assessment of melanocytic lesions.

title: Deep learning of point-of-care lung ultrasound and clinical data for pulmonary tuberculosis triage in Uganda
abstract: Rationale: Point of care lung ultrasound is portable and radiation free and could extend tuberculosis screening to settings without chest radiography, but no standardized criteria exist for interpreting it for tuberculosis. Objectives: To develop and internally evaluate deep learning models that classify pulmonary tuberculosis from lung ultrasound images, alone and combined with routine clinical variables, and to derive an abbreviated scanning protocol. Methods: In a prospective study in Kampala, Uganda (2023 to 2025), we enrolled people aged 13 years or older with microbiologically confirmed pulmonary tuberculosis, their household contacts, and symptomatic people with other respiratory conditions. One still frame from each of 12 lung ultrasound zones was analyzed with an attention-based multiple-instance learning network. We compared clinical-only (random forest), ultrasound only, and combined models and derived a 6 zone protocol from training set attention weights. Participants were allocated to training (n = 223), validation (n = 20), and held-out test (n = 73) sets. Results: Of 318 enrolled participants, 316 were analyzed (118 with and 198 without tuberculosis). In the test set, areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve were 0.88 (95% confidence interval, 0.80 to 0.95) for the clinical-only model; 0.93 (0.86 to 0.97) and 0.95 (0.89 to 0.99) for the 12 zone ultrasound-only and combined models; and 0.91 (0.83 to 0.97) and 0.93 (0.86 to 0.99) for the corresponding 6-zone models. At 90% sensitivity, specificity was 82.2% (34.9 to 97.8) for the 12-zone combined model and 91.1% (25.0 to 98.0) for the 6-zone combined model. Point estimates for all 12-zone models and the 6-zone combined model met the 2025 World Health Organization minimum accuracy targets for a high-sensitivity screening test (≥90% sensitivity, ≥60% specificity). Conclusion: Lung ultrasound analyzed with attention-based deep learning and combined with clinical variables showed high internal discrimination for pulmonary tuberculosis, and a simplified 6-zone protocol retained most of this performance. External validation in intended-use screening populations is needed

title: Rapid screening of target-specific isotope labeling protocols for in situ NMR of bacterial membrane proteins
abstract: We describe an approach for the efficient development of targeted isotope labeling protocols leading to nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) structural studies of bacterial membrane proteins in intact cells and native outer membrane (OM) vesicles (OMVs). The assay relies on the bioorthogonal non-canonical amino acid tagging (BONCAT) approach for metabolic incorporation of an azide-bearing residue, followed by copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) to an alkyne-functionalized fluorescent dye. Fluorescence detection in SDS-PAGE provides a rapid way to test samples for off-target background signal from endogenous proteins, bypassing the need for intensive NMR screening experiments. Using this approach, we develop an optimized protocol that enables high-resolution NMR spectra to be obtained in situ with negligible background signal. The BONCAT approach also enables target-specific fluorescence or nano-gold labeling of proteins at the OM surface, further extending the utility of this protocol for correlative structure-activity studies of membrane proteins in situ.

title: Traumatic microbleeds are associated with unfavorable outcome out to 1 year after mild traumatic brain injury
abstract: Importance: Traumatic microbleeds (TMB) are commonly observed in mild TBI (mTBI). However, questions remain regarding their long-term prognostic significance. Objective: Determine whether traumatic microbleeds predict unfavorable outcome after mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) Design: The prospective longitudinal observational Transforming Research and Clinical Knowledge in Traumatic Brain Injury (TRACK-TBI) study enrolled acute TBI patients presenting to Emergency Departments (ED) at 18 U.S. Level 1 trauma centers between 2/26/2014-08/08/2018. CT and MRI were evaluated using the National Institutes of Health National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH NINDS) TBI Common Data Elements. Outcome was assessed using the Glasgow Outcome Scale Extended (GOSE-TBI) at 2 weeks and 3, 6, and 12 months post-injury. Setting: 18 U.S. Level 1 trauma centers Participants: 929 GCS 13-15 patients at least 17 years of age (38.5 +/- 16.5 years, 66% male) who underwent clinical head CT <24 hours after injury and brain MRI at 2 weeks post-injury and had at least one GOSE-TBI outcome score during 1 year follow-up. Exposure(s): Acute non-penetrating head trauma Main Outcome(s) and Measure(s): Frequency and co-occurrence of CT and MR features; incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI <8 vs. 8) and unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI <5 vs. >=5) at 2 weeks and 3, 6, and 12 months Results: Generalized estimating equation models showed that TMBs and/or IVH were strongly associated with unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI <5 vs. >=5) at 3, 6, and 12 months post-injury, but not with incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI <8 vs. =8). For prediction of GOSE-TBI <5 vs. >=5 TMBs surpassed the importance of all demographic and baseline clinical predictors throughout the 1-year follow-up period. For prediction of incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI <8 vs. =8), brain contusions, subarachnoid hemorrhage, and subdural hematoma were more important throughout the 12-month follow-up period. Conclusions and Relevance: Traumatic microbleeds (TMB) are common in mTBI. The presence of 4 or more TMBs and/or IVH is strongly associated with unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI <5) after mTBI out to at least 1 year, even after controlling for other neuroimaging abnormalities and demographic and clinical predictors. Better understanding of the implications of TMBs for long-term functional outcome may inform rehabilitation planning.

Determine whether traumatic microbleeds predict unfavorable outcome after mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) Design: The prospective longitudinal observational Transforming Research and Clinical Knowledge in Traumatic Brain Injury (TRACK-TBI) study enrolled acute TBI patients presenting to Emergency Departments (ED) at 18 U.S. Level 1 trauma centers between 2/26/2014-08/08/2018. CT and MRI were evaluated using the National Institutes of Health National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH NINDS) TBI Common Data Elements. 18 U.S. Level 1 trauma centers Participants: 929 GCS 13-15 patients at least 17 years of age (38.5 +/- 16.5 years, 66% male) who underwent clinical head CT <24 hours after injury and brain MRI at 2 weeks post-injury and had at least one GOSE-TBI outcome score during 1 year follow-up. title: Manifestation-Guided Adaptation of CT Foundation Model for Early Neurological Prognosis after ECPR
abstract: PurposeTo develop a data-efficient, clinically guided transfer-learning framework for hyperacute neurological outcome prediction from head CT in patients undergoing extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) after cardiac arrest by leveraging free-text radiology report. MethodsThis retrospective study included 683 patients with available CT examination and radiology reports from December 2015 to November 2025. The primary outcome distinguished favorable neurological outcomes (Cerebral Performance Category [CPC] 1-2) from neurological death due to brain death or cerebral herniation (CPC 5). A cross-attention adaptor jointly learned to predict neurological outcome and five report-derived manifestations of brain injury from a frozen pretrained head CT encoder. Outcome prediction used CT images alone at inference. The manifestation-guided adaptor, trained with and without additional patients who contributed only manifestation labels, was compared with outcome-only adaptor and two pooled-feature baselines. Performance was summarized as mean {+/-} SD across five held-out folds. ResultsOf 683 patients, 197 were eligible for outcome evaluation (63 with favorable outcomes and 134 with neurological death), and 486 formed the manifestation-only cohort. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.918 {+/-} 0.044 for the outcome-only adaptor. The manifestation-guided adaptor achieved an AUROC of 0.927 {+/-} 0.042. With additional manifestation-only training data, the adaptor achieved the mean AUROC (0.929 {+/-} 0.037), specificity (93.7% {+/-} 6.5%), with a sensitivity of 79.9% {+/-} 9.2%. ConclusionManifestation-guided adaptation outperforms outcome-only adaptation for neurological outcome prediction from hyperacute head CT after ECPR. Report-derived manifestation labels enabled training with additional examinations without eligible outcome labels while preserving CT-only prediction.

title: Age and sex differences in lateral ventricle choroid plexus volume in a large, manually segmented, multi-site MRI dataset
abstract: Background The choroid plexus, which produces cerebrospinal fluid and forms the blood–cerebrospinal fluid barrier, is of growing interest in psychiatric and neurodegenerative neuroimaging. However, most volumetric studies have relied on automated segmentation tools that agree poorly with manual tracing, and manually segmented samples have been small, single-site, and narrow in age range. Methods We analyzed DataPlex, a dataset of 700 manually segmented lateral ventricle choroid plexus labels from 3T T1-weighted MRI scans (ages 6–90 years) drawn from 29 studies and three scanner manufacturers (35 study-by-manufacturer sites). Generalized least squares models accounting for within-site dependence tested associations of age, sex, scanner manufacturer, image resolution, a registration-based image-quality metric, and intracranial volume with choroid plexus and lateral ventricle volumes, including nonlinear (spline) and sex-interaction terms. Exploratory models tested associations between these volumes and cognitive performance. Results In 699 scans, choroid plexus volume increased linearly with age (63–69 mm³ per decade) and was 56–65 mm³ larger in males than females after covariate adjustment; the age association did not differ by sex. Lateral ventricle volume increased nonlinearly with age, with steeper age-related enlargement in males than females. Scanner manufacturer and image resolution were associated with left lateral ventricle volume; scanner manufacturer was associated with choroid plexus volume only in a sensitivity model. The image-quality metric was not associated with any outcome. In exploratory analyses, larger choroid plexus volume was associated with lower inhibitory control, working memory, and episodic memory scores and with higher emotion recognition scores (uncorrected p < 0.05). Conclusions In the largest and most diverse manually segmented choroid plexus dataset to date, choroid plexus volume differed by age and sex and was less sensitive than lateral ventricle volume to acquisition differences. These estimates provide reference benchmarks for automated segmentation tools and support adjustment for demographic and technical covariates.
